The checker also validates local assets and redirects; it does not make network requests to external sites.

Keep normal repository-relative links in Markdown. docs/hooks.py converts links that leave docs/ into GitHub source links at DOCS_SOURCE_SHA during rendering. A local preview without that variable links to main. The recipe checkout command in the installation guide is pinned to that source SHA; other code samples are not rewritten. Every PR builds the site in CI and retains a documentation-preview artifact, including when only documentation changes.

docs.title: Versions and source identity
docs.text:
Trigger Published location Meaning Push to main develop/ Unreleased development documentation Stable numeric tag X.Y.Z X.Y.Z/ Documentation from that exact tag Prerelease tag such as X.Y.Zrc1 X.Y.Zrc1/ Candidate documentation, not stable Local mkdocs build or serve Local output Unpublished preview

Each generated page names its channel and links its exact source commit. versions.json records the source SHA and channel for each published version. Only the highest stable numeric Git tag may move latest; prereleases and lower maintenance releases leave it unchanged. The root initially opens develop and switches to latest once stable documentation is published. Old version trees are preserved rather than rebuilt with new tooling.

Older package releases that predate this workflow are not relabeled with current content. Their documentation remains in their tagged source. A documentation tag and successful site deployment do not prove that the corresponding PyPI upload succeeded: verify the package release separately. Pushing any tag also triggers the existing PyPI release workflow. Never push a test tag to exercise docs.

docs.title: How publishing works
docs.text:
.github/workflows/deploy-doc.yml runs on main and tag pushes. Its manual action can recover a deployment for an existing main or tag ref; it does publish. It uses Python 3.12 and the locked docs group. The workflow:

  1. Fetches the existing gh-pages archive and builds the selected version locally with mike. Mike's temporary staging commits never enter published history.
  2. Checks the complete versioned tree's links, anchors, assets, redirects, and version manifest before making an archive update.
  3. Writes the checked tree to gh-pages through GitHub's createCommitOnBranch API and requires a valid GitHub signature. The expected parent SHA prevents overwriting a concurrent update. No local mike commit is pushed.
  4. Uploads that same checked tree to GitHub Pages and deploys it through the github-pages environment. The documentation-site artifact retains the checked tree for 14 days; permanent version history lives on gh-pages.

Unlike spark-on-k8s's legacy branch publishing, this repository uses GitHub's Pages artifact deployment. This permits signed archive commits without a stored private signing key and does not rely on a bot branch push triggering another workflow. Alias pages are regular redirect files, not symlinks.

Deployment runs share a concurrency group. An active run is not cancelled, but GitHub retains only one pending run: rapid pushes can replace a pending tag run. Inspect the run list after releases and rerun a displaced tag publication when needed. Archive compare-and-swap failures stop rather than force-pushing.

docs.title: Initial repository setup
docs.text:
This is a one-time maintainer setup, not part of ordinary documentation edits:

  • Enable GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions as the source. The project inherits the account's hussein.awala.fr domain; do not add a project CNAME file.
  • Create an empty gh-pages branch with a signed commit and verify its signature before pushing it. Do not branch it from main with the package source files.
  • Allow the github-pages environment to deploy from main and intended version tags, keeping any existing maintainer protection rules. The workflow requires contents write permission for its archive job and Pages/OIDC permissions for its deployment job.

The workflow deliberately fails if the archive or Pages configuration is absent. It does not silently create unsigned history or change repository settings. No additional token or signing-key secret is needed: publication uses the workflow's scoped GITHUB_TOKEN and GitHub's commit signature.

docs.title: Verify or recover a deployment
docs.text:
Check both jobs of the exact Deploy documentation run. Then verify the public version manifest at https://hussein.awala.fr/async-batcher/versions.json, the new version's home page, channel label, and source link against the workflow SHA. The latest/ alias changes only for an eligible stable version.

A successful archive update can precede a failed Pages deployment. In that case, the public site may still show its previous content. Inspect the failed job and rerun the existing workflow for the intended ref after fixing the cause. A deployment job refuses an artifact superseded by a newer archive commit; use the current main run to publish the complete updated archive in that case. Do not move release tags or create a new package release to repair documentation. If an archive API request has an ambiguous outcome, inspect gh-pages and its manifest before retrying. A conflicting or unsigned archive result is a publishing failure, not permission to force-push or bypass signature verification.

docs.title: Shared release notes
docs.text:
Release notes are a project-wide page independent of the selected documentation version. Every version's navigation links to that permanent URL. Main deployments rebuild it from release-notes/*.md; tag deployments preserve its existing archive bytes, so an older release cannot replace newer history. It is not an entry in the documentation version selector.

Each file contains metadata followed by the canonical GitHub release body. Published 0.2.0, 0.2.1, and 0.2.2 bodies were copied from GitHub, preserving their wording and normalizing line endings. Planned releases are labeled In preparation. To preview:

uv run --no-sync python .github/scripts/release_notes.py build --output-dir release-notes-site
uv run --no-sync python .github/scripts/check_docs.py release-notes-site --base-path /async-batcher/release-notes/

Before creating an authorized GitHub release, export its reviewed body rather than maintaining a second copy. For example:

uv run --no-sync python .github/scripts/release_notes.py extract 0.3.0 --output /tmp/async-batcher-0.3.0-notes.md

Use that file with the existing release process's --notes-file argument. Extraction only writes a local file; it does not publish. After package and GitHub publication are confirmed, update the file's status, date, and github_url to the actual release in a signed documentation PR. Its main deployment updates the shared page without rebuilding archived version docs. Preserve historical bodies; release-note corrections should be deliberate and reviewed.

docs.title: Save embeddings before delivering vectors
docs.text:
The durable handoff recipe separates two operations:

  1. Read an immutable JSONL file, obtain embeddings, validate each entire model response, and commit the vectors to a local SQLite spool.
  2. Read pending vectors from that spool, upsert them to the destination, and mark acknowledged rows.

Retrying stage 1 reuses embeddings already committed for the same job. Retrying stage 2 reads saved vectors and never calls a model. This is an application recipe, not a persistent queue in AsyncBatcher. The two stages run sequentially, so disk must hold the full set of embeddings before delivery starts.

docs.title: Run without credentials
docs.text:
The example lives in the repository, outside the installed package. From the matching recipe checkout:

uv sync --locked --no-default-groups --python 3.12
uv run --no-sync python -m examples.recipes.durable_embeddings \
  --input /tmp/documents.jsonl --spool /tmp/embedding-spool.sqlite \
  --sink /tmp/delivered-vectors.sqlite --job-id catalog-v1

Input lines contain exactly nonempty string id and string text fields. IDs must be unique within the file. This demo uses deterministic text features, not semantic embeddings, and a SQLite vector sink without similarity search. Run the same command again after interruption. It prints counts of persisted embeddings, acknowledged vectors, and vectors still pending. A completed rerun scans the source for identity/reuse checks but sends neither new model calls nor completed upserts.

docs.title: Bind identity before paying for work
docs.text:
Spool(database, job_id, Identity(...)) requires explicit provider, model, revision, preprocessing, input type, vector dimension, and destination identity. Use a destination identifier that includes index/namespace/tenant as appropriate; never put credentials in it. Initialization binds the job to that complete configuration plus the immutable file's SHA-256 and byte length. A configuration or source mismatch fails before any embedding call. An identical source copy can use a different path.

Each spool row also stores its source byte offset, document ID, text digest, validated vector, and acknowledgement state. There is no cross-job cache, eviction policy, or raw-text copy in the spool. Vectors, IDs, and configuration can still be sensitive. Protect the database and its backups.

These identities are application declarations. They cannot prove that a remote client actually uses the named model/revision, preprocessing, tenant, or destination. Configure those clients consistently and use genuinely pinned model behavior when reproducibility matters. If a provider changes a model behind an unchanged name, this recipe cannot detect that change. Duplicate IDs within a dispatch are rejected before calling the model; a later duplicate can be discovered after earlier embedding costs.

docs.title: Use application-owned providers
docs.text:
stage_file(path, spool, model, executor=pool) borrows a model with async embed(texts) -> list[list[float]]. deliver_pending(spool, sink, executor=pool) borrows a sink with async upsert(records) -> list[str], where each VectorRecord has an ID and saved vector. The sink must return every input ID in order and must converge when the same ID and vector are replayed. Client/model contexts must outlive these helpers and their accepted work. Keep the caller-owned thread pool alive and join it after the event loop, as the CLI does.

For a Cohere/Pinecone application, adapt the existing provider recipe: pass texts to CohereEmbedder, extract its validated vector values, and upsert VectorRecord values to the already compatible Pinecone index/namespace. Validate the index dimension before starting stage 1, as that recipe does. Choose count/byte/token limits for those actual providers; the generic spool example does not impose their quotas or wire-size constraints. Local tests exercise the native Cohere HTTP and Pinecone SDK boundary, including a lost acknowledgement after a committed write.

Run only one application worker per job, and finish stage 1 before stage 2. There is no distributed lease, concurrent-producer protocol, background worker, or automatic retry loop. Different job IDs have separate local rows; destinations can still conflict if those jobs use the same remote IDs.

docs.title: Recovery boundaries
docs.text:
• Crash after the embedding transaction commits: stage 1 finds the saved vectors and skips those calls.
  • Crash/lost response before embedding persistence: that paid call may need repeating. The spool cannot recover an embedding response it never durably received.
  • Sink failure, lost response, or crash before the local acknowledgement update: vectors remain pending. Stage 2 may replay a write the sink already committed. Stable upserts converge; exactly-once delivery and a transaction spanning local/remote systems are not provided.
  • Cancellation: map intake closes and accepted work drains. It can commit more vectors/acknowledgements than the caller observed. Keep clients open through drain, and join worker threads.
  • Invalid model output: wrong counts, dimensions, nonnumeric or nonfinite values fail the entire dispatch before any of that response is saved. Earlier committed embeddings remain usable.

The source is hashed in one-MiB chunks and read in chunks of at most 32 lines, each at most 64 KiB. Both stages use one active batch, a default batch size of 32, and a map window of 64. Delivery reads pages of at most that window; one page can be retained in addition to the map's pending items. Vectors consume dimension-dependent memory, and disk use grows with the complete job. Monitor available disk and define your own retention policy. No automatic deletion occurs.

SQLite uses WAL and synchronous=FULL; storage must honor synchronization. Keep the database/WAL files together and use SQLite-aware backups on a supported local filesystem. Source checks detect ordinary mutation, not adversarial filesystem races. acknowledged_vectors records the sink's acknowledgement contract, not immediate search visibility or independent proof of remote durability.

docs.title: DynamoDB reads and writes
docs.text:
Install the aws extra for Async Batcher 0.3.0; see installation for Python requirements and release availability:

python -m pip install 'async-batcher[aws]==0.3.0'
The adapters use aioboto3 resource values: Python strings, integers/Decimal, bytes, lists, and dictionaries, rather than low-level AttributeValue wrappers. Floats are not supported by boto3's DynamoDB serializer.

import asyncio

from async_batcher.aws.dynamodb.get import AsyncDynamoDbGetBatcher, GetItem
from async_batcher.aws.dynamodb.write import AsyncDynamoDbWriteBatcher, WriteOperation


async def write_then_read():
    # Configure AWS credentials normally; the table and its Key partition key must exist.
    writer = AsyncDynamoDbWriteBatcher(region_name="us-west-2")
    reader = AsyncDynamoDbGetBatcher(region_name="us-west-2", consistent_read=True)
    try:
        await asyncio.gather(
            writer.process(WriteOperation(operation="PUT", table_name="test-table", data={"Key": "one"})),
            writer.process(WriteOperation(operation="PUT", table_name="test-table", data={"Key": "two"})),
        )
        return await asyncio.gather(
            reader.process(GetItem(table_name="test-table", key={"Key": "one"})),
            reader.process(GetItem(table_name="test-table", key={"Key": "two"})),
        )
    finally:
        await asyncio.gather(writer.stop(), reader.stop())

Reads return an item dictionary or None for a missing item. Requests for the same table must use the same primary-key attribute names. Duplicate keys are deduplicated for the service call and mapped back to every caller. The response order from DynamoDB does not affect caller order.

Writes accept WriteOperation(operation="PUT", ...) with a full item or operation="DELETE" with its key. They return None; deleting a missing item succeeds. Conditional writes and updates are outside this batch API. Repeated operations on the same item in a write batch are not deduplicated and can be rejected by DynamoDB.

docs.title: Limits, ownership, and retries
docs.text:
Read max_batch_size defaults to 100 and accepts 1–100; write defaults to 25 and accepts 1–25. The count applies across all tables in the dispatch. Other core options are available. AWS can also reject requests for byte limits or invalid keys.

Both adapters accept region_name, endpoint_url, use_ssl, verify, config, and an optional aioboto3_session. TLS is enabled by default. Each dispatch opens and closes its own DynamoDB resource context from that session; there is no client for the caller to close through the batcher. Use the local FastAPI example to avoid contacting AWS.

Unprocessed keys/items are retried up to max_retries times after the first request (default 5; 0 disables retries). Backoff starts at 0.1 seconds and caps at 5 seconds. Exhaustion raises DynamoDBRetryError, available from async_batcher.aws.dynamodb.exceptions, for the whole dispatch. Previously completed writes are not rolled back, and partial read results are not returned when the dispatch fails. SDK retries are configured separately on the client/session.

docs.title: Read consistency
docs.text: Reads are eventually consistent by default. consistent_read=True applies strongly consistent reads to every requested table and is preserved for unprocessed-key retries. Strong reads have different capacity costs; see DynamoDB read consistency.

docs.title: Projected reads
docs.text:
Use projection_expression and optional expression_attribute_names to select fields for every requested table. Include every primary-key attribute as a complete top-level field so the adapter can map unordered responses, including duplicate requests. It validates this before opening a connection and does not insert hidden fields into the returned projection.

from async_batcher.aws.dynamodb.get import AsyncDynamoDbGetBatcher

reader = AsyncDynamoDbGetBatcher(
    projection_expression="#pk, #sk, details.#name, tags[0]",
    expression_attribute_names={"#pk": "partitionKey", "#sk": "sortKey", "#name": "name"},
)

Nested paths and list indexes are forwarded to DynamoDB but do not count as complete key fields. The alias mapping is copied at construction; retries preserve projection and aliases. Without a projection, reads return all attributes. A projection reduces returned data, not read capacity consumption.

docs.title: FastAPI lifespan, predictions, and SQLite writes
docs.text:
This runnable app creates one prediction batcher and one SQLite writer during FastAPI startup. Lifespan closes intake before attempting graceful drain, with optional bounded escalation to force cleanup. It uses a deterministic weighted sum as a demo predictor, not a trained model, and real SQLite transactions for writes. No model download, server account, or credentials are needed.

The example dependencies are an opt-in development group. They are not added to the core package or any adapter extra. The application itself lives in the repository. From the matching recipe checkout:

uv sync --locked --group example-test --python 3.12
BATCHER_DEMO_DATABASE=/tmp/batcher-web.sqlite \
  uv run --no-sync uvicorn examples.recipes.fastapi_app:demo_app --factory \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --workers 1

Keep that process running and use another terminal:

curl --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"features":[1,2,3]}'
curl --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8000/documents \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"id":"example-1","text":"Stored in SQLite"}'
curl --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8000/metrics

/predict returns {"score":2.3} for this input. /documents returns HTTP 201 and the stored ID. The same ID updates its previous value. Each write batch has its own transaction; several HTTP requests are not one global transaction. The database path persists across restarts; choose a new path when you need an empty demo database.

The input models require three finite numeric features between -1,000,000 and 1,000,000, and document IDs of 1–128 characters with text up to 4,096 characters. Invalid bodies return HTTP 422 before reaching a batcher. These are demonstration bounds, not a limit on the entire HTTP body: set appropriate request-body and connection limits in your serving infrastructure too.

docs.title: Batch concurrent requests and inspect measurements
docs.text:
Sequential curl commands normally form single-item batches. This bounded cohort sends 32 requests concurrently and prints actual client elapsed time plus the server's aggregated batch sizes. Run it with uv run --no-sync python from the same checkout:

import asyncio
import time

import httpx2


async def main():
    async with httpx2.AsyncClient(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000", timeout=5) as client:
        started = time.perf_counter()
        responses = await asyncio.gather(
            *(client.post("/predict", json={"features": [1, 2, 3]}) for _ in range(32))
        )
        for response in responses:
            response.raise_for_status()
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
        print({"completed_requests": len(responses), "elapsed_seconds": elapsed})
        metrics = await client.get("/metrics")
        metrics.raise_for_status()
        print(metrics.json())


asyncio.run(main())

/metrics reads stats() on the owning event loop and aggregates on_batch completion events. It returns counts and actual batch-size histograms, with no request payloads. Values accumulate since this app's lifespan started, including earlier requests. They are JSON diagnostics, not a Prometheus endpoint. See observability for exporter integration.

Client elapsed time includes HTTP overhead and the chosen demonstration workload; it is not a benchmark speedup claim. There are no performance thresholds in CI. The tests make real in-process HTTP requests to FastAPI and verify SQLite rows, batched responses, overload, failures, and cleanup.

docs.title: Capacity, failures, and ownership
docs.text:
The defaults are 16 items per batch, 64 waiting items per queue, one active batch per batcher, and a 10 ms collection delay. The SQLite writer also has a 64 KiB encoded ID/text cost budget. The budget is an estimate of submitted payload, not serialized request size or process memory.

HTTP handlers use the default immediate queue-admission policy. A full queue returns HTTP 503 with Retry-After: 1 and does not enqueue that request. The header is an illustrative retry delay; clients should bound retries and apply backoff. Accepted requests continue independently. A backend exception, including a backend TimeoutError, remains HTTP 500 instead of being described as a full queue. Use stable IDs and understand backend side effects before retrying a failed write.

Waiting admission is available through process(..., wait_for_space=True), but waiting HTTP handlers still occupy server resources. Choose server concurrency limits and a clear timeout policy before enabling it; max_queue_size alone does not bound external waiting producers. max_queue_time is a collection delay, not a handler deadline.

When lifespan shutdown starts, the app rejects late submissions instead of restarting a drained child. It waits for accepted work to finish before clearing application state. Cancelling an HTTP handler does not retract a backend write; caller cancellation and shutdown are not rollback guarantees. The CLI demo waits up to two seconds for each response (504 on expiry), then permits five seconds for graceful shutdown and one second for force cleanup. create_app defaults those three optional settings to None; choose explicit budgets for your application. A response timeout does not stop accepted backend work. A force-cleanup timeout is surfaced instead of silently ignored. See operational deadlines for backend timeouts, server/supervisor budgets, and thread ownership: running synchronous functions cannot be interrupted by cancelling asyncio tasks.

create_app(database, prediction_processor=...) can inject a real bulk function. Regular functions run in the thread executor; async functions must avoid blocking the event loop. Load application-owned models/clients in lifespan before entering the batcher contexts, then close them after those contexts finish. The example does not close a separately supplied model/client callable on the caller's behalf. Each SQLite operation owns and closes its own connection in its worker thread.

These limits and metrics apply per application process. Multiple Uvicorn workers create separate batchers, while SQLite still serializes database writes. Use the single-worker command above for the demo; choose a database and worker configuration appropriate to the deployment. The streaming cookbook shows bounded background producers and a two-stage embedding pipeline.

docs.title: Run the HTTP checks
docs.text:
uv sync --locked --group example-test --python 3.12
uv run --no-sync python -m pytest tests/examples -ra

Core-only test discovery does not import FastAPI. CI installs the optional group explicitly and checks imports before running the HTTP suite, so an unexpectedly missing dependency cannot silently skip the expected job. TestClient is used as a context manager for lifespan startup/shutdown; async HTTPX2 tests explicitly enter the registered lifespan because ASGITransport does not do so. See the official FastAPI lifespan guide, lifespan testing guide, and HTTPX ASGI transport lifecycle.

docs.title: Batch an existing function
docs.text:
These APIs require Async Batcher 0.3.0; see installation. AsyncBatcher.from_callable() accepts a bulk function and all normal batcher options. There is no need to subclass when you already have a function that processes a list.

import asyncio
from async_batcher import AsyncBatcher


async def double_many(values: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    return [value * 2 for value in values]


async def main():
    async with AsyncBatcher.from_callable(double_many, max_batch_size=8) as batcher:
        results = await asyncio.gather(*(batcher.process(i) for i in range(20)))
        print(results)


asyncio.run(main())

The function receives one positional list argument. Async functions, bound async methods, partials of async functions, and objects with an async __call__ execute on the event loop. Regular functions execute in the configured thread executor, with the same context propagation as synchronous subclass processors. If a regular function returns an awaitable (for example, a decorator wraps an async function), the wrapper awaits that result on the event loop. Async generators are not supported. Forced shutdown cannot interrupt a running thread; a fresh coroutine returned after cancellation is closed without being executed. A custom awaitable can provide a synchronous close() method for this cleanup. Other custom awaitables and already-running tasks remain processor-owned after cancellation: the wrapper does not invoke __await__ or cancel borrowed tasks.

Return one result per input in order, or None for a write-only operation. Existing error and result rules apply, including per-item exceptions. The wrapper owns neither an explicitly provided executor nor clients used by your function.

docs.title: Managed lifecycle
docs.text:
Every batcher, including existing subclasses and adapters, supports async with. Entering binds the event loop but does not start processing. Exiting drains accepted work even if the body raised an exception or was cancelled, then propagates that exception. It does not retry failed requests or roll back external writes. Await request tasks to observe their errors; shutdown itself does not re-raise per-item failures.

Nested or concurrent context entries for the same batcher are rejected. A completed context can be entered again on the same event loop. Exit has no implicit timeout; for custom timeout or forced cancellation policies, use explicit stop() calls. If the exit wait itself is cancelled, accepted work continues draining under the existing stop() contract.

Keep client or executor contexts outside the batcher context, so resources remain available until its work has finished. As with explicit shutdown, do not exit the batcher's context from its own processor or one of that processor's child tasks.

docs.title: Group compatible requests
docs.text:
GroupedBatcher routes each item to a child batcher chosen by a synchronous, hashable group_key. Use separate groups for different models, destinations, or processing options. A child only receives items with the same key.

import asyncio
from async_batcher import AsyncBatcher, GroupedBatcher


def make_batcher(destination: str) -> AsyncBatcher[tuple[str, int], int]:
    async def write_many(items: list[tuple[str, int]]) -> list[int]:
        # Replace with the destination's real bulk operation.
        assert all(item[0] == destination for item in items)
        return [item[1] for item in items]

    return AsyncBatcher.from_callable(write_many, max_batch_size=100)


async def main():
    async with GroupedBatcher(
        make_batcher, group_key=lambda item: item[0], max_groups=16, idle_timeout=30
    ) as grouped:
        print(
            await asyncio.gather(
                grouped.process(("orders", 1)),
                grouped.process(("events", 2)),
                grouped.process(("orders", 3)),
            )
        )


asyncio.run(main())

The factory runs on the event loop and must return a fresh, unused AsyncBatcher for each key. It can return an adapter or use from_callable() as above. Both callbacks must be synchronous and quick. Reusing a child across keys is rejected. Groups isolate batches, not credentials or authorization; choose keys that fully capture compatibility requirements.

docs.title: Resource bounds
docs.text:
max_groups is a positive integer (default 128). It counts children that are processing, idle, or still shutting down. When the cap is reached, the least recently idle group is stopped before its slot is reused. If every group has outstanding work, process() raises GroupLimitError; it does not queue an unbounded number of new groups. Applications can wait and resubmit or reject.

idle_timeout is a finite nonnegative number of seconds (default 60); zero starts cleanup as soon as a group becomes idle. Idle groups are automatically stopped and removed. A new request for a group currently closing waits for that cleanup before creating a replacement. Cancellation of that wait leaves cleanup running. group_count includes children still closing.

Batch size, queue size, and concurrency are configured by the factory per group. With 16 groups and child concurrency 2, up to 32 batches may run. Use finite child queue limits as well as the group cap to bound application memory.

docs.title: Cancellation and shutdown
docs.text:
Cancelling a grouped caller stops its wait; its child request continues and keeps the group busy until it settles. This prevents eviction from losing track of accepted work. It does not undo side effects. This differs from cancelling a direct AsyncBatcher.process() caller, which cancels its result future.

await grouped.stop() permanently closes the manager, rejects new submissions, and drains all children. A custom child shutdown failure leaves its group tracked and keeps its capacity occupied; a later stop() can retry cleanup. stop(force=True) requests child cancellation and waits for cleanup. A later forced call can escalate an ongoing graceful stop. Timeouts and cancellation of stop waiters leave shutdown running; await stop() again to join it. Running thread functions retain the core's cancellation limitations.

The async context manager drains on exit, including after a body exception, and does not suppress that exception. Nested entry is rejected. Unlike an individual batcher, a stopped group manager cannot restart: create a new manager. Factories and their clients remain caller-owned; close shared clients after the manager. Do not stop the manager from a child processor or its descendant tasks.

docs.title: Flush accepted child work without closing the manager
docs.text:
await grouped.flush(timeout=None) dispatches partial batches and waits for work already accepted by every currently owned child, including children already closing. Intake stays open. Each child's acceptance boundary is captured when the grouped flush coroutine starts, before its child waiters are scheduled. Later submissions to existing or new keys cannot extend those boundaries.

await grouped.flush(timeout=5)

This is the same acceptance boundary as core flush. Manager reservations still waiting for group eviction or child queue admission are excluded, even if grouped.pending_items already counts them. Scheduling a process() coroutine also does not prove child acceptance. A flush does not create groups, cancel eviction, or free group slots early. It keeps references to its selected children while waiting; replacement children and later work do not enter the boundary. Use stop() to close intake and drain the manager's owned requests, including admission waits, when ending the service lifecycle.

Completion includes child batch cleanup and completion hooks, even if a grouped caller stopped waiting. It does not assert that each request succeeded or that an external write is durable; inspect the individual results or map_outcomes() for failures. Ordinary item errors do not fail flush. timeout must be finite and nonnegative; its expiration raises TimeoutError. Timeout or cancellation abandons only this flush wait and leaves accepted work running. Forced shutdown of an included child interrupts flush with RuntimeError, including if that shutdown occurs between snapshotting and starting the child waiters. Other child work is not cancelled by this interruption. Graceful shutdown can finish a flush normally.

An empty flush binds the manager's event loop without creating children. A flush after completed shutdown returns immediately; it does not reopen the manager. A processor or its active descendants cannot flush their own manager because that would wait for themselves.

docs.title: Bounded grouped streams and child admission
docs.text:
grouped.process(item, wait_for_space=True, enqueue_timeout=0.5) forwards those admission options to the selected child. The timeout covers that child's queue admission only, not group eviction or processing. By default a full child queue still raises QueueFullException. If all group slots are busy, a new key still raises GroupLimitError immediately even when waiting admission is enabled; this option does not create a queue of unbounded new groups.

grouped.map(source, max_pending=128, ordered=True) and grouped.map_outcomes(...) provide the same bounded input consumption, ordering and source cleanup as the corresponding core stream methods. They use waiting admission for child queues. A busy group limit fails map() promptly and becomes a correlated error in map_outcomes(). Choose max_groups for the number of concurrently active keys or handle rejected outcomes explicitly.

Use contextlib.aclosing when breaking early. Closing or cancelling a grouped stream closes its source and joins its own mapping tasks, but leaves the manager and unrelated users open. Once a request is handed to a child, the group manager keeps owning its child task through completion, including an admission wait. Thus cancellation does not withdraw that child submission: it may still be admitted and executed later. Stop the group manager to drain or force-stop all its work.

docs.title: Aggregate accepted-item cap
docs.text:
Set max_pending_items to a positive integer to bound owned submissions across all groups; None (the default) leaves this aggregate bound disabled. pending_items reports the current count. A reservation starts when the manager accepts a call, before key lookup/group eviction, and continues through child admission and processing until that child task completes. These manager reservations are not the child's accepted-item statistics. Pre-child failure or cancellation returns its reservation; a cancelled caller with an owned child does not.

An exhausted aggregate cap raises QueueFullException immediately, even with wait_for_space=True. Waiting remains child-queue-only; enqueue_timeout does not wait for an aggregate reservation. In a grouped map_outcomes, rejected reservations are ordinary indexed failures; in map, they terminate iteration. Set the cap for all concurrent users, not just one map's window, or explicitly handle overload. max_groups still independently bounds child instances. Closing/cancelling a map does not free permits for its still-owned child requests; stop() drains those requests and stop(force=True) requests cancellation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: These instructions target Async Batcher 0.3.0, which requires Python 3.11 or newer. Check the shared release notes for publication status. The documentation banner identifies release, prerelease, and development pages; use the version matching your package.

docs.title: Install the package
docs.text:
In your application's virtual environment:

python -m pip install 'async-batcher==0.3.0'

With a uv-managed application:

uv add 'async-batcher==0.3.0'

The core has no runtime dependencies. Run Python examples with python demo.py, or uv run python demo.py in a uv-managed application. You do not need to clone this repository to use the core API or adapters. See your first batch.

For an upgrade, read migration from 0.2.2, keep the extras your application needs, and test its configuration, shutdown, and backend error handling.

docs.title: Run the repository recipes
docs.text:
The runnable modules under examples/recipes/ and the older applications under examples/ are repository examples. They are not installed by the wheel. To run them, obtain the source matching the docs, then use its locked environment:

git clone https://github.com/hussein-awala/async-batcher.git
cd async-batcher
git checkout --detach 0118bf3fc72f117e2f7dd30bed53df246e741eee
uv sync --locked --no-default-groups --python 3.12

Published documentation pins this checkout command to its exact source commit. When reading the Markdown directly on GitHub, choose the published tag or a reviewed commit. The 0.3.0 tag becomes available when that release is published. A development preview can use the source commit linked in its banner before the tag exists.

Run a recipe from the repository root, for example:

uv run --no-sync python -m examples.recipes.sqlite_stream --help

Follow the selected guide's additional sync command for HTTP or provider dependencies. uv sync replaces the selected environment; uv run --no-sync keeps it unchanged. Legacy Keras/gRPC applications have separate README instructions and environments. Core and adapter application code can use the PyPI package without these example files.

docs.text: Source builds, tests, typing checks, live service setup, and documentation previews are described in Contributing. Those workflows use uv and uv.lock; they are separate from installing the library into an application.

docs.title: Kafka producer batches
docs.text:
Install the kafka extra for Async Batcher 0.3.0; see installation for Python requirements and release availability:

python -m pip install 'async-batcher[kafka]==0.3.0'
Use AsyncKafkaBatcher with a caller-owned aiokafka producer. The adapter collects application requests into native Kafka batches and groups them by an explicit topic and partition. The caller supplies and starts the producer:

import asyncio

from aiokafka import AIOKafkaProducer
from async_batcher.kafka import AsyncKafkaBatcher, KafkaRecord


async def publish():
    producer = AIOKafkaProducer(bootstrap_servers="localhost:9092", enable_idempotence=True)
    await producer.start()
    batcher = AsyncKafkaBatcher(producer=producer, max_batch_size=100, max_queue_time=0.01)
    try:
        results = await asyncio.gather(
            *(
                batcher.process(KafkaRecord(topic="events", partition=0, value=value))
                for value in (b"first", b"second")
            )
        )
        print([(result.partition, result.offset) for result in results])
    finally:
        try:
            await batcher.stop()
        finally:
            await producer.stop()


asyncio.run(publish())

KafkaRecord accepts topic, partition, key, value, timestamp_ms (epoch milliseconds), and headers (string/bytes-or-None pairs). A keyed value=None is a tombstone. Choose partitions in your application; the adapter does not invoke the producer's partitioner. Key/value objects use the supplied producer's serializers, which must be deterministic: a record can be serialized again when it fills one native batch and is retried in the next.

The batcher's max_batch_size counts records. The producer's max_batch_size limits native batch bytes; full builders are sent before remaining records are appended to a new builder. aiokafka can accept an oversized first record into an otherwise empty builder. That record is sent alone, and a broker size rejection fails that record without discarding successful neighboring batches. max_queue_size and max_queue_time have the usual AsyncBatcher meanings. Keep concurrency=1 (the default) to retain per-partition order across separate application batches.

Each request returns its own aiokafka RecordMetadata, including its offset and timestamp. CreateTime uses the individual record's timestamp; LogAppendTime uses the broker's timestamp. Unknown offsets/timestamps remain unknown. With acks=0, the result is None and delivery is unconfirmed. Validation, serialization, enqueue, and broker failures affect their corresponding records; asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) lets callers inspect partial successes. The adapter does not retry whole application batches or roll back successful records.

The caller owns producer start/stop, retries, acknowledgements, serializers, and transactions. Stop the batcher before stopping the producer. Cancellation or stop(force=True) cannot retract records already accepted by Kafka; pending producer deliveries continue and may succeed after the caller is cancelled. Avoid blind resubmission when the delivery outcome is unknown.

See core lifecycle and live test setup.

docs.title: Prediction adapters
docs.text: These examples require Async Batcher 0.3.0; see installation. The adapters accept the core limits and executor options. Submit one sample per process() call. Both invoke synchronous model.predict in an executor and return the corresponding prediction. The model remains caller-owned. Keep the default concurrency=1 unless your model and backend can safely predict concurrently; more threads do not necessarily improve throughput.

docs.title: Keras
docs.text:
The keras extra requires Keras 3.15.1 or newer and a separately installed backend. This example uses JAX; install and select it before importing Keras:

python -m pip install 'async-batcher[keras]==0.3.0' jax
export KERAS_BACKEND=jax

Save this example as keras_demo.py and run python keras_demo.py:

import asyncio

import keras
from async_batcher.ml.keras.model import KerasAsyncBatcher


async def main():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(2,))
    model = keras.Model(inputs, keras.layers.Rescaling(2.0)(inputs))
    batcher = KerasAsyncBatcher(model=model, max_batch_size=32)
    try:
        predictions = await asyncio.gather(batcher.process([1.0, 2.0]), batcher.process([3.0, 4.0]))
        assert predictions[0].tolist() == [2.0, 4.0]
        assert predictions[1].tolist() == [6.0, 8.0]
    finally:
        await batcher.stop()


asyncio.run(main())

Inputs are combined with numpy.asarray(batch) along a new leading batch axis. Supply one dense sample with consistent shape, not an already batched array. Multiple-input, ragged, and custom input structures require a custom process_batch implementation.

Tensor outputs are split along their leading batch axis. Dictionary, list, and tuple outputs retain their nested structure for each caller; every tensor leaf must have one row per input. A malformed output fails the entire batch.

Keras also supports TensorFlow and PyTorch; follow its backend installation guide and validate your model on the chosen backend. Keras 2 is unsupported. Prefer the native .keras model format for new models. The bundled legacy HDF5 example loads with compile=False, and its inference path is tested with JAX; custom layers and other backends need separate validation. See the Keras 3 migration guide.

Runnable application examples: FastAPI and gRPC.

docs.title: scikit-learn
docs.text:
Install python -m pip install 'async-batcher[sklearn]==0.3.0'. Supply a fitted estimator with a predict method:

import asyncio

from async_batcher.ml.sklearn.model import SklearnAsyncBatcher
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression


async def main():
    model = LinearRegression().fit([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0]], [0.0, 2.0, 4.0])
    batcher = SklearnAsyncBatcher(model=model, max_batch_size=32)
    try:
        predictions = await asyncio.gather(batcher.process([3.0]), batcher.process([4.0]))
        assert abs(predictions[0] - 6.0) < 1e-8
        assert abs(predictions[1] - 8.0) < 1e-8
    finally:
        await batcher.stop()


asyncio.run(main())

Dense feature rows are passed as a batch. If any input is a SciPy sparse vector or single-row matrix, all inputs are stacked as CSR without densifying sparse data; dense rows can be mixed into that batch. Each input must represent exactly one sample. Sparse predictions remain CSR rows with shape (1, n_outputs); dense predictions follow the estimator's per-sample output shape. Missing predict, invalid shapes, and prediction errors fail the batch. Training and model mutation remain application responsibilities; finish them before submitting predictions.

Both prediction wrappers forward additional core options, including max_batch_cost, item_cost, and on_batch. A cost function receives each original sample before dense stacking or sparse conversion, so it can estimate work from feature count, nonzero entries, or application-specific input size. The count limit still applies alongside the cost limit. Batch completion hooks run synchronously on the event loop, after prediction outcomes are assigned; keep them short even though prediction itself runs in an executor. Core validation rejects invalid options and oversized samples before prediction.

docs.title: Upgrade from 0.2.2 to 0.3.0
docs.text: Async Batcher 0.3.0 adds public APIs and adapters while retaining the existing subclass interface and configuration defaults. Review the compatibility changes below before upgrading an application. The shared release history records publication status and release notes; use the version selector for the docs matching your installation.

docs.title: What changes
docs.text:
Capability 0.2.2 0.3.0 Python minimum 3.10 3.11 Subclass AsyncBatcher, implement process_batch, submit with process Available Available, with stricter result/configuration validation from_callable and async context managers Not available Functions and cleanup Bounded map, map_outcomes, waiting admission, flush Not available Streams and flush Cost budgets, statistics, groups, coalescing Not available API guide and linked composition guides DynamoDB, Scylla, SQLAlchemy, Keras, scikit-learn extras Older SDK requirements Updated SDK requirements and corrected result/failure behavior Kafka, MongoDB, Pinecone, Kinesis/Firehose adapters Not available Installation and adapters Contributor environment Poetry uv with the committed uv.lock

Install the selected version, retaining the extras your application uses:

python -m pip install --upgrade 'async-batcher==0.3.0'
# For example, an AWS application:
python -m pip install --upgrade 'async-batcher[aws]==0.3.0'

The installation guide covers application environments and optional clients. For an application staying on 0.2.2, pin async-batcher==0.2.2 and use its tagged documentation.

docs.title: Upgrade an application deliberately
docs.text:
1. Move the application and its CI to Python 3.11 or newer. Check each optional SDK's supported interpreters and install only the extras the application needs.
  2. Keep existing subclass processors if they suit the application. Return one result per input in order, or None for all-None results. Current validation rejects unordered/unsized containers, strings, bytes, and incorrect result counts before reporting any success from that collection. Returning an exception at a result position fails that caller; it does not roll back backend writes.
  3. Check constructor arguments. Invalid numeric limits and unknown options now fail explicitly. Replace deprecated batch_size with max_batch_size; sleep_time and buffering_time have no effect. max_batch_size=1 is supported. Choose finite queue, batch, and concurrency limits for production; max_queue_size=0 still means unlimited, not disabled.
  4. Put batcher cleanup inside the lifetime of its clients and executors. An async context manager drains accepted work even on exceptional exit. Caller cancellation does not prove that a write was prevented. A shutdown timeout leaves cleanup in progress; keep dependencies open and await cleanup again. See the lifecycle contract before changing restart behavior.
  5. Recheck adapter output, transaction, partial-error, and retry contracts against its guide. SQLAlchemy now requires 2.0.10+; its bulk updates require mapped ORM models and primary keys, and reject Core Table updates and UPDATE RETURNING. Keras requires 3.15.1+; Keras 2 is no longer supported. Install and validate the chosen Keras backend separately. DynamoDB uses TLS by default and applies bounded retries to unprocessed requests. SDK upgrades and corrected result mapping can expose assumptions in application code. Test duplicate IDs, missing results, partial failures, and replay using your own payload shapes.
  6. Run application tests against the pinned candidate. For a stream, prefer bounded map over creating one task for every input. For a service, test overload and shutdown while work is active. The starting configurations illustrate both paths.

Automatic restart belongs to a fully stopped AsyncBatcher on its original event loop. Grouped managers and coalescing wrappers close permanently. Do not move existing instances between loops or mutate their construction-time limits to reconfigure a running service.

New context, logging, cancellation-discard, grouping, and coalescing options are opt-in. Adopt them only with the corresponding ownership and compatibility rules; an upgrade does not require using every feature. Keep a pinned previous application environment available for rollback.

docs.title: Operational statistics and batch events
docs.text: The core exposes immutable BatcherStats and BatchEvent dataclasses. It does not depend on a monitoring client, collect item payloads, or start an exporter. Read these APIs from the same event-loop thread that owns the batcher. These APIs require Async Batcher 0.3.0; see installation for the matching package and optional extras.

docs.title: Read a snapshot
docs.text:
import asyncio

from async_batcher import AsyncBatcher, BatcherStats


class Doubler(AsyncBatcher[int, int]):
    async def process_batch(self, batch: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        return [item * 2 for item in batch]


async def main():
    batcher = Doubler(max_batch_size=8)
    try:
        assert await batcher.process(3) == 6
    finally:
        await batcher.stop()
    stats: BatcherStats = batcher.stats()
    assert stats.accepted == stats.succeeded == 1
    assert stats.pending_items == stats.active_batches == 0


asyncio.run(main())

stats() returns a new snapshot. Reading it does not bind an event loop, reset counters, or change an earlier snapshot. It examines outstanding accepted futures, so its cost grows with outstanding work; use periodic sampling instead of reading it for every item. Futures that completed but whose bookkeeping callbacks have not run yet are included in terminal totals.

Field Meaning queued_items Entries waiting for collection, including a retained item that would exceed the preceding batch's cost limit. Includes already-cancelled requests until the dispatcher removes their entries. admission_waiters Producers currently waiting for queue capacity. These are not accepted work. Cancellation, timeout, or shutdown removes each waiter when its admission coroutine exits. oldest_pending_seconds Age since acceptance of the oldest unresolved result, or None when none remain. Includes partial batches and active processing; excludes admission waits and work whose callers already cancelled. state idle before starting, running while the dispatcher is active, stopping during shutdown cleanup, and stopped after cleanup. A later submission restarts a stopped batcher. This does not track executor functions that outlive forced cancellation. pending_items Accepted requests whose result futures are not terminal, including items currently collected into a partial batch. in_flight_items Items in dispatched batch workers until their completion cleanup finishes. Includes requests whose callers have already cancelled. active_batches Dispatched batch workers awaiting completion cleanup. accepted Lifetime requests admitted to the input queue. rejected Lifetime submissions refused because the queue is full, an admission wait times out, or shutdown interrupts/refuses admission on the owning loop. Invalid arguments/costs and foreign-loop calls are excluded. succeeded, failed, cancelled Lifetime terminal outcomes of accepted result futures, counted once each. batches_dispatched, batches_completed Lifetime batch workers created and batch completion cleanups finished.

Totals survive graceful stop, forced stop, and automatic restart. They reset only when a new batcher is constructed. Every snapshot satisfies:

accepted = pending_items + succeeded + failed + cancelled
batches_dispatched = active_batches + batches_completed

The gauges describe different stages and must not be added together. A partially collected batch can have pending items but no queued or in-flight items. A running batch can have in-flight items but no pending results after its callers cancel. Cancellation describes the result delivered to the caller: a synchronous backend function can still finish after forced shutdown. A cancelled request does not later become a success in these statistics. Work cancelled before admission is not accepted and contributes no terminal outcome or rejection. A producer waiting for capacity is not yet accepted and contributes only to admission_waiters.

docs.title: Receive completion events
docs.text:
Pass on_batch at construction. It receives one event for each dispatched batch, after resource cleanup and request outcomes are settled. No event is emitted for items cancelled while still queued or collected if they never become a dispatched batch. Events can arrive in completion order rather than dispatch order when concurrency exceeds one.

from async_batcher import BatchEvent

completed_batches: list[BatchEvent] = []


def on_batch(event: BatchEvent) -> None:
    completed_batches.append(event)


# Using the Doubler subclass above:
batcher = Doubler(max_batch_size=8, on_batch=on_batch)

The list is a small demonstration; use a bounded sink or aggregate metrics in a long-running application. Every event contains only these fields:

  • batch_id: a monotonically increasing dispatch identifier for this batcher, retained across restarts.
  • size: actual number of input entries passed to the batch worker.
  • queue_wait_seconds: oldest item's time from acceptance to processing start. If the worker never starts, this is its time from acceptance to completion cleanup instead. Busy processors can make residence exceed max_queue_time; it is not a per-item latency distribution.
  • processing_seconds: processor execution and result-validation time, excluding the observer. It is None if the worker was cancelled before it started. For a cancelled executor await, this measures the batch worker's wait, not the eventual duration of the still-running backend function.
  • succeeded, failed, cancelled: per-item result-future outcomes, summing to size.

Events contain no items, results, exception objects, request IDs, or user labels. Their outcome totals cover dispatched batches only; use stats() for all accepted requests, including queued cancellations. A returned per-item exception counts as failure, a returned CancelledError as cancellation, and a whole-batch processor/result-validation exception fails unresolved requests.

The callback runs synchronously on the event-loop thread and must finish quickly. Do not perform network I/O, block, await shutdown, or create an unbounded task for every event. Ordinary callback exceptions are logged without changing request results. KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, and other BaseException subclasses are not swallowed. Cleanup happens before invocation.

Async functions, async generators, and objects with async __call__ are rejected at construction. If a synchronous wrapper unexpectedly returns an awaitable, it is logged as misuse: a coroutine is closed, and an explicit synchronous close() on a custom awaitable is called when available. The library never invokes a custom __await__() or awaits asynchronous cleanup. Custom resources without that synchronous cleanup protocol remain the callback owner's responsibility. Returned asyncio futures/tasks are left running because the observer might have borrowed them; their eventual exceptions are retrieved to avoid unobserved-error warnings. They remain the callback owner's responsibility. Such return values are unsupported; the hook must return None.

docs.title: Optional Prometheus recipe
docs.text:
Install prometheus-client in your application, then connect an inexpensive in-process callback. Keep exporter/server setup in the application's lifecycle. Choose histogram buckets for the actual workload; the following are illustrative. See the official instrument types and histogram API.

from prometheus_client import Counter, Gauge, Histogram

from async_batcher import BatchEvent

queue_depth = Gauge("batcher_queue_items", "Waiting input entries")
duration = Histogram(
    "batcher_processing_seconds",
    "Batch worker processing time",
    buckets=(0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10),
)
outcomes = Counter(
    "batcher_dispatched_item_outcomes_total",
    "Outcomes in completed dispatched batches",
    ["outcome"],
)


def prometheus_batch(event: BatchEvent) -> None:
    if event.processing_seconds is not None:
        duration.observe(event.processing_seconds)
    for outcome in ("succeeded", "failed", "cancelled"):
        outcomes.labels(outcome=outcome).inc(getattr(event, outcome))


def sample_queue_on_owner_loop(batcher) -> None:
    queue_depth.set(batcher.stats().queued_items)


# Construct once: Doubler(on_batch=prometheus_batch).
# Call sample_queue_on_owner_loop periodically from your application's event loop.

Do not call stats() from a Prometheus HTTP server's scraping thread. Sample on the owning loop, then let the metrics client expose the recorded values. Use a small fixed set of labels, not payload values or batch IDs. Recreating instruments repeatedly in one registry can cause duplicate registration errors; define them once for the application or use separate registries.

docs.title: Optional OpenTelemetry recipe
docs.text:
Configure an application-owned SDK MeterProvider and exporter before obtaining the meter; the API alone does not export data. The official Python instrumentation guide and metrics API describe provider setup and instruments. No OpenTelemetry package is required by this library.

from opentelemetry import metrics

from async_batcher import BatchEvent

meter = metrics.get_meter("example.batcher")
processing = meter.create_histogram("batcher.processing", unit="s")
completed = meter.create_counter("batcher.dispatched.items", unit="1")


def otel_batch(event: BatchEvent) -> None:
    if event.processing_seconds is not None:
        processing.record(event.processing_seconds)
    for outcome in ("succeeded", "failed", "cancelled"):
        completed.add(getattr(event, outcome), {"outcome": outcome})


# Construct once: Doubler(on_batch=otel_batch).

Keep export work off the hook's critical path through your SDK's configured reader/exporter. If collecting batcher gauges through an SDK callback running on another thread, first copy a snapshot on the owning loop and let that callback read the immutable copy. The same outcome scope and cancellation limitations apply to both recipes.

docs.title: Exception details in logs
docs.text:
Completion events contain no payloads, but processors and observers can raise exceptions whose messages contain input values. The default log_exceptions=True includes those messages, chained causes, and tracebacks in error logs.

Set log_exceptions=False on a batcher to emit only fixed failure messages. The original exception still reaches its caller; application logging of that exception requires its own policy. Set the option on both GroupedBatcher and its child factory to cover manager cleanup and processing failures respectively. This controls library error records, not logs produced by a client, model, or user callback.

docs.title: Deadlines, shared capacity, and telemetry
docs.text: The operational helpers are application recipes in the repository, outside the installed package. They use the standard library and core contracts. Set up the matching recipe checkout, then run the examples with uv run --no-sync python from its root.

docs.title: Give each deadline one job
docs.text:
Budget What expires What it does not guarantee Collection: max_queue_time Waiting to form a batch An end-to-end response or backend deadline Admission: enqueue_timeout with waiting enabled Waiting for queue capacity A timeout after the request has been accepted HTTP response: Intake.process(response_timeout=...) This caller's wait, including queueing and processing Retraction of accepted work, rollback, or interruption of a worker thread Async backend: backend_call(..., timeout=...) One cancellation-cooperative async bulk call Backend rollback, a hard execution limit for blocking code, or a timeout per item Deployment: Intake.shutdown(grace_timeout=..., force_timeout=...) Graceful drain, then waiting for forced cleanup Termination of threads or the whole process within that sum

ResponseDeadlineExceeded and BackendDeadlineExceeded are distinct. The helper checks whether its own timeout context expired; an ordinary TimeoutError raised by the backend is preserved. Timeout cancellation requires cooperative async code and can wait for that code's cleanup. See Python's timeout contract.

This runnable example closes intake before drain and keeps the exporter alive until batch callbacks have finished. The backend and exporter are explicit local demonstrations, with no network calls:

import asyncio
from dataclasses import asdict

from async_batcher import AsyncBatcher
from examples.recipes.operations import BoundedExporter, Intake, backend_call


async def demo_backend(items):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return [item * 2 for item in items]


async def processor(items):
    return await backend_call(demo_backend, items, timeout=0.5)


async def demo_export(event):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)  # Replace with a bounded async monitoring-client call.


async def main():
    async with BoundedExporter(demo_export, max_events=16) as exporter:
        batcher = AsyncBatcher.from_callable(
            processor, max_batch_size=4, max_queue_size=16, on_batch=exporter.observe
        )
        intake = Intake(batcher)
        try:
            results = await asyncio.gather(*(intake.process(item, response_timeout=1) for item in range(8)))
            print(results)
        finally:
            await intake.shutdown(grace_timeout=2, force_timeout=1)
    print(asdict(batcher.stats()))
    print({"telemetry_sent": exporter.sent, "failed": exporter.failed, "dropped": exporter.dropped})


asyncio.run(main())

Choose positive finite timeout values from your own backend and deployment budgets. None disables the intake/backend/shutdown timeout; the telemetry exporter instead requires finite positive budgets. If force cleanup also times out, Intake.shutdown raises and keeps intake closed. Cleanup can still be running. Keep references to the batcher and its resources; retry stop(force=True) when appropriate, or let the process supervisor enforce its separate termination policy. Do not silently reopen intake or close a client while surviving work still needs it.

docs.title: Apply the policy to HTTP
docs.text:
The FastAPI app exposes separate response and shutdown settings:

from pathlib import Path

from examples.recipes.fastapi_app import create_app
from examples.recipes.operations import backend_call


async def demo_predict(rows):
    return [sum(row) for row in rows]  # Demo only, not a trained model.


async def timed_predict(rows):
    return await backend_call(demo_predict, rows, timeout=0.5)


app = create_app(
    Path("/tmp/batcher-deadlines.sqlite"),
    prediction_processor=timed_predict,
    response_timeout=1,
    shutdown_grace=5,
    shutdown_force=1,
)

This HTTP example requires uv sync --locked --group example-test. Serve the app as described in the FastAPI guide. Full queues return 503 without accepting the item; a configured response/backend deadline returns 504 with a distinct explanation. An unrelated backend exception, including its own TimeoutError, remains 500. Stable IDs and backend-specific retry rules still matter after any ambiguous failure.

Both child intakes close before either child starts draining. Their shutdown attempts run together; errors are surfaced as an exception group after both attempts finish. The CLI demo uses a two-second response wait, five-second graceful drain, and one-second force-cleanup wait. create_app itself defaults those settings to None, so callers choose their own policy.

The ASGI server's connection drain and your supervisor's process-termination grace are additional budgets. Account for startup/shutdown hooks, exporter drain, and backend/client cleanup too. Setting an HTTP response deadline alone does not bound application shutdown. Use backend-native socket, query, and transaction deadlines as applicable; cancelling an executor await does not add them. See Uvicorn's shutdown behavior when configuring that server alongside the application policy.

docs.title: Share backend capacity across groups
docs.text:
A child's concurrency applies only to that child. Eight groups at concurrency two can attempt sixteen calls. Pass the same semaphore to async_groups to cap cancellation-cooperative async backend calls across every child, or across multiple managers that share it:

import asyncio

from examples.recipes.operations import async_groups


async def demo_bulk(tenant, items):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return [(tenant, value * 2) for _, value in items]


async def main():
    backend_slots = asyncio.Semaphore(2)
    async with async_groups(
        demo_bulk,
        group_key=lambda item: item[0],
        backend_slots=backend_slots,
        max_groups=4,
        batch_size=2,
    ) as groups:
        cohort = [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("a", 3), ("b", 4)]
        print(await asyncio.gather(*(groups.process(item) for item in cohort)))


asyncio.run(main())

This finite cohort is a demonstration. Keep real producers bounded too: a semaphore limits calls inside the backend section, not the number of waiting producer tasks or per-group queue memory. Each child queue here holds at most 64 waiting items and max_groups bounds children. A semaphore is a concurrency limit, not a rate limiter. It does not itself implement fairness between tenants.

For synchronous processors, share a bounded caller-owned executor instead. Keep its context outside asyncio.run, so its actual threads join before the surrounding client resources close:

import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

from examples.recipes.operations import thread_groups


def demo_bulk(tenant, items):
    return [(tenant, value * 2) for _, value in items]


async def main(pool):
    async with thread_groups(
        demo_bulk, group_key=lambda item: item[0], executor=pool, batch_size=2
    ) as groups:
        print(await asyncio.gather(*(groups.process(item) for item in [("a", 1), ("b", 2)])))


with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
    asyncio.run(main(pool))
# A caller-owned backend client can close after the pool has joined.

Forced batcher shutdown can return while a submitted synchronous function still runs. Never release a backend semaphore immediately on coroutine cancellation and assume its thread stopped: that can permit more actual backend work than intended. The shared executor caps simultaneously executing threads even in that case. Its internal submission queue is not a producer backpressure policy; retain group, queue, and pending limits. Joining the pool may outlast a deployment budget if its functions do not finish. Use backend-native timeouts/cooperative cancellation, or a separately supervised process for work that must be terminable; the batcher does not own this decision.

docs.title: Export metadata without blocking batch completion
docs.text:
BoundedExporter.observe only enqueues an immutable, payload-free BatchEvent with put_nowait. It does not do network I/O, wait for capacity, or create a task per event. One worker drains at most max_events queued events plus one in-flight event. Keep the exporter context outside batchers so their final completion callbacks can still enqueue.

  • sent counts successful callback returns, not an independently verified durable delivery.
  • failed counts send exceptions and send deadlines; the worker continues with later events.
  • dropped counts overflow, events offered outside its active lifetime, and unsent events discarded when shutdown expires. Counted loss is intentional: these diagnostics are not a durable audit log.

The async send callback must cooperate with cancellation and use its own bounded I/O operations. Exporter shutdown first attempts a bounded drain, then cancels the sender and counts queued losses. A client that suppresses cancellation or blocks the event loop defeats cooperative deadlines. Expose the counters through your application monitoring without adding request payloads, secrets, or high-cardinality tenant IDs to labels. See core observability.

docs.title: Pinecone vector batches
docs.text:
Install the pinecone extra for Async Batcher 0.3.0; see installation for Python requirements and release availability:

python -m pip install 'async-batcher[pinecone]==0.3.0'
The extra requires Pinecone SDK 10.3 through 10.x. The vector adapters use a caller-owned pinecone.AsyncIndex and one namespace per batcher:

  • AsyncPineconeUpsertBatcher: accepts SDK Vector objects (dense, sparse or hybrid), returning None when the server acknowledges the write.
  • AsyncPineconeFetchBatcher: accepts vector IDs and returns SDK Vector objects or None for missing IDs, preserving input order and duplicate requests.
  • AsyncPineconeDeleteBatcher: accepts vector IDs and returns None after a successful call. Deleting a missing ID also succeeds.
import asyncio

from pinecone import AsyncIndex, Vector
from async_batcher.pinecone import AsyncPineconeUpsertBatcher


async def write_vectors(host: str):
    # The SDK reads PINECONE_API_KEY from the environment.
    async with AsyncIndex(host=host) as index:
        batcher = AsyncPineconeUpsertBatcher(index=index, namespace="articles")
        try:
            await asyncio.gather(
                batcher.process(Vector(id="one", values=[0.1, 0.2, 0.3])),
                batcher.process(Vector(id="two", values=[0.4, 0.5, 0.6])),
            )
        finally:
            # Drain accepted work before the caller closes the shared index.
            await batcher.stop()

Use your index's actual vector dimension. These adapters target the SDK's vector interface, not schema-based document indexes. They batch upserts, fetches and deletes; similarity queries and partial updates remain direct SDK operations.

Each dispatch makes one native SDK call. max_batch_size defaults to 100 and must be between 1 and 1,000. All three batchers require IDs of 1–512 ASCII characters without NUL. Upserts also have a 2 MB request limit; large vectors or metadata need a smaller batch size. SDK validation, size and service errors fail that dispatch, with no extra adapter retries or rollback. Duplicate upsert IDs within one dispatch are rejected before writing; use concurrency=1 (the default) for sequential dispatches, or separate awaited writes when repeatedly replacing the same ID. Fetches and deletes deduplicate IDs within a dispatch.

Writes are eventually consistent: an acknowledgement does not guarantee immediate visibility in a subsequent fetch or query, and deletion success does not establish that an ID existed. The caller owns the index and must keep it open until every batcher using it has stopped. The adapters never create, enter, or close the index.

See core lifecycle and test setup.

docs.title: Compose provider pacing and finite retries
docs.text:
The provider-policy recipe is application-owned policy around an async bulk call. AsyncBatcher still owns count/cost collection, bounded producer admission, and batch concurrency. It does not gain automatic retry or rate-limit behavior.

The example lives in the repository, outside the installed package. Run the local, credential-free demonstration from the matching recipe checkout:

uv sync --locked --no-default-groups --python 3.12
uv run --no-sync python -m examples.recipes.provider_policy

The demo doubles integers and deliberately rejects its first attempt. It reports actual results, provider attempts, retry attempts, and throttled responses; these are not billing measurements.

docs.title: One shared budget for the actual provider attempts
docs.text:
Create one Pacer(requests_per_second=..., units_per_second=...) per provider quota scope and share it across every relevant child/group/caller. A ProviderPolicy borrows that pacer and wraps an async operation with await policy.run(operation, units=estimated_work, total_timeout=60).

The pacer spaces call starts by the larger of 1 / requests_per_second and estimated_work / units_per_second. The optional units can represent conservatively estimated tokens or other work. The first call can start immediately; it charges the interval before the next call. There is no accumulated burst credit. Every attempt spends its interval, including rejected, failed, and subsequently cancelled calls. A cancelled waiter does not reserve a new slot.

This is conservative application pacing, not a model of every provider's rolling/calendar windows, actual token accounting, daily limits, or other clients using the same account. Enforce per-request count/token/byte caps separately and leave headroom for estimation error. An oversized single request is not made valid by a longer interval. A shared pacer controls starts, not simultaneously running calls, memory, tenant fairness, or cross-process quotas. Keep bounded maps/queues and shared backend capacity limits from the operations guide.

docs.title: Classify retryable rejections explicitly
docs.text:
The policy catches only Throttled. Translate a provider's documented rejection to that type only when your application permits replay of that operation. It does not catch arbitrary HTTP errors, transport errors, backend timeouts, cancellation, or failed writes.

For an HTTPX2 client, an application bulk operation can classify a response like this:

from examples.recipes.provider_policy import Pacer, ProviderPolicy, Throttled

pacer = Pacer(requests_per_second=2, units_per_second=1000)
policy = ProviderPolicy(pacer, max_attempts=3, base_delay=0.5, max_delay=30)


async def bulk_call(client, payload, estimated_tokens):
    async def attempt():
        response = await client.post("/your-bulk-endpoint", json=payload)
        if response.status_code == 429:
            raise Throttled(response.headers.get("Retry-After"))
        response.raise_for_status()
        return response.json()

    return await policy.run(attempt, units=estimated_tokens, total_timeout=60)

This snippet borrows an already configured client; the endpoint/payload and response-to-input mapping remain application-specific. Do not treat every 429 from an arbitrary service as proof that no billable work or side effect occurred. For saved embeddings and replayable vector writes, see the durable handoff recipe; ambiguous writes still need backend-specific recovery.

max_attempts includes the first call. Missing or invalid Retry-After uses exponential full jitter, with a ceiling of max_delay. A valid integer-seconds or HTTP-date header supplies a minimum delay, following HTTP Retry-After semantics. The policy uses the larger of that minimum and local jitter. Normal cooldowns extend the shared pacer, so other waiting calls recheck them too, even after the last allowed attempt. Already running calls cannot be recalled. An HTTP-date depends on the machine's wall clock being reasonably synchronized.

If a server requests more than max_delay, the call fails immediately with Throttled; its request is never retried sooner by shortening that header to the cap. Stop or defer application intake as appropriate for such a response; this refusal does not install a permanent account-wide circuit breaker. The Throttled message omits provider payloads, but its header attribute and caller-owned client exceptions still need your logging policy.

total_timeout covers pacing, retries, backoff, and the async operation together. It relies on cooperative cancellation and is not a hard process deadline. Client-native I/O timeouts remain useful. Cancelling during backoff sends no new attempt; cancelling after a provider call starts does not undo its work. attempts, retry_attempts, and throttled_responses count actual entered attempts across this policy instance, not map results, all SDK-internal requests, or charged tokens.

docs.title: Give retries one owner
docs.text:
For this HTTPX2 pattern, configure AsyncHTTPTransport(retries=0) so transport attempts are not hidden inside the application retry loop. Keep client contexts outside the batcher and finish batcher drain before closing the client. Bound the total operation budget as well as individual I/O budgets.

An SDK may retry by itself. The Cohere/Pinecone recipe already documents Pinecone's native retries. Keep those SDK retries as their sole owner, or explicitly configure/verify the SDK to perform one attempt before adding application retries. Do not blindly wrap a retrying SDK and multiply its retry count. This recipe changes neither that provider example nor any adapter's retry policy.
