docs.title: Import valid records and retain explicit rejections
docs.text:
The rejected-record recipe imports an immutable JSONL file into SQLite, while recording invalid input as source locations and fixed reason codes. The original streaming and resumable importers remain fail-fast.

The example lives in the repository, outside the installed package. From the matching recipe checkout:

uv sync --locked --no-default-groups --python 3.12
uv run --no-sync python -m examples.recipes.rejected_import \
  --input /tmp/documents.jsonl --database /tmp/reviewed-import.sqlite --run-id review-1

Valid lines contain exactly a nonempty string id and a string text. Invalid UTF-8/JSON, invalid fields, and lines above 64 KiB become one rejection each. An oversized line is drained in bounded pieces through its real newline; its suffix is never treated as another record. Offsets are zero-based UTF-8 byte positions, including line endings. A final line need not end in a newline.

A rejection stores run_id, starting/ending byte offsets, and one of invalid_utf8_or_json, invalid_document_fields, or line_too_large. It does not store the rejected payload or decoder exception. The run stores the source path and SHA-256 digest; valid documents retain their text. Keep the original source if rejected records need review, and protect both source and database.

The reader deliberately yields success/rejection envelopes instead of raising for known input errors. map_outcomes() alone would not do this: source iteration errors still terminate that iterator. Filesystem errors, changed source contents, and SQLite failures still stop this recipe. They are not classified as bad records and are never silently skipped or retried.

docs.title: Bounds and transaction ownership
docs.text:
The reader buffers at most 32 lines of 64 KiB each. Rejected oversized lines retain only metadata. A bounded map retains at most 64 submitted/unconsumed rows by default, and the writer uses one 32-row batch at a time. No list of all successes or rejected records is accumulated in memory. The initial SHA-256 scan uses one-MiB chunks. These bounds exclude SQLite's own caches and Python object overhead; use application-specific sizes before increasing them.

Each transaction atomically stores its audit rows and valid document upserts. Duplicate IDs within one run overwrite earlier values in source order. The output counts input records, not unique IDs. A database failure rolls back its entire batch while earlier transactions remain committed.

Inspect rejections with an application-owned SQLite client:

SELECT r.source_path, r.sha256, x.start, x.end, x.rejection
FROM rejected_import_rows AS x JOIN rejected_import_runs AS r USING (run_id)
WHERE x.run_id = 'review-1' AND x.rejection IS NOT NULL ORDER BY x.start;

Use a fresh run ID for every invocation; reuse fails even if the earlier run was interrupted. Rows from different runs are isolated. This example does not implement resume, automatic repair, or a transaction across the entire file. For atomic resume of valid immutable input, use the separate resumable recipe; do not edit a failing source and reuse its checkpoint.

Cancellation closes the map and drains accepted writes, so more rows may commit than the caller observed. The caller owns the shared thread pool and must join it before releasing resources; the CLI does that after the event loop finishes. Connections use WAL and synchronous=FULL; durability still depends on storage honoring synchronization. Keep SQLite database/WAL files together and use a supported local filesystem. Source-change checks detect ordinary mutation, not adversarial races.

docs.text:
These development checks run from the same recipe checkout:

uv sync --locked
uv run --no-sync python -m pytest tests/core/test_rejected_import_recipe.py -q

docs.title: Resume a JSONL import after a crash
docs.text:
This runnable recipe extends the basic SQLite writer with a durable checkpoint. It requires only the core package and Python's standard library. It does not change the library's batching API or turn an entire import into one transaction.

Each JSONL line must contain exactly a nonempty string id and a string text:

{"id": "document-1", "text": "First document"}
{"id": "document-2", "text": "été 🌎"}

The example lives in the repository, outside the installed package. From the matching recipe checkout, run:

uv sync --locked --no-default-groups --python 3.12
uv run --no-sync python -m examples.recipes.resumable_sqlite \
  --input /tmp/documents.jsonl --database /tmp/import.sqlite --job-id catalog-v1

After interruption, run the same command with the same job ID. A completed import reads no more records, although it still hashes the file to verify its identity. The report includes the prior processed count, this run's acknowledged results, total committed records, byte checkpoint, elapsed import time, actual batch-size histogram, and batcher statistics. Elapsed time excludes the initial whole-file identity scan and schema/checkpoint initialization; it is not a speedup claim.

docs.title: What is atomic
docs.text:
One SQLite transaction performs both operations:

  1. Upsert a contiguous batch of records into import_documents, keyed by job ID and document ID.
  2. Advance that job's byte offset and processed-record count in import_jobs.

A row failure rolls back the entire batch, including its checkpoint. Earlier batches remain committed. If the process dies after commit but before it receives the batch results, the next run resumes after those records. Tests exercise this window with a real subprocess exit. Duplicate IDs overwrite earlier values in file order; the processed count counts input records, not distinct document IDs. Different job IDs have separate document rows.

The writer uses one batch at a time and BEGIN IMMEDIATE. Every batch checks that its first offset matches the saved checkpoint and that subsequent offsets are contiguous. A stale concurrent importer fails with CheckpointConflict; it cannot advance the job past records it did not write. Run one importer per job. Other SQLite writers can still contend for the database's write lock; the connection uses a five-second busy timeout, not an end-to-end import deadline.

Every worker call owns and closes its SQLite connection. Connections explicitly enable WAL mode, synchronous=FULL, and foreign keys. WAL plus FULL synchronizes each commit; durability still depends on the filesystem and storage honoring SQLite's synchronization requests. Keep the database and its WAL files together, use a supported local filesystem, and use SQLite-aware backup procedures. See SQLite's synchronization documentation and WAL restrictions. This checkpoint covers only these SQLite rows, not external API calls or other databases.

docs.title: Immutable input and bounded memory
docs.text:
The first run binds the job ID to the file's SHA-256 digest and byte length. Every restart hashes the full source again in one-MiB chunks; a changed file is rejected even when its size is unchanged. An identical copy can resume the same job from a different path. For new content, choose a new job ID deliberately. To recover a failed existing job, restore the original file rather than edit out the bad line and reuse its checkpoint.

Keep the source immutable throughout the run. The recipe checks file identity, size, and modification timestamps before and after reads and before commits to detect ordinary replacement or mutation. These checks are not a filesystem snapshot or protection against an adversary deliberately racing file changes. For a live producer, first publish a completed immutable file or use a transactional message source instead.

Record validation errors identify the filename and zero-based byte offset of the failing line. Their messages and normal traceback chains omit record contents and decoder exception details. Paths themselves can be sensitive; apply your application logging policy.

Offsets count UTF-8 bytes, including line endings, so multibyte text and a final line without a newline resume correctly. Blank lines, invalid UTF-8/JSON, extra fields, and invalid IDs are rejected. The reader buffers at most 32 records, each limited to 64 KiB including its newline, beyond the map's default 64 pending items. Parsing a later invalid line may discard that unsubmitted chunk; the saved checkpoint still identifies the last committed prefix. Reading ahead never advances it.

The caller owns a shared two-thread executor for hashing, reading, and writing. Cancellation closes the map and gracefully drains already accepted writes; it can therefore leave more committed rows than the caller observed. An asyncio cancellation does not kill a Python worker thread. The CLI joins the pool after the event loop exits, including any cancelled read or hash operation. For a hard deployment deadline, close intake and apply a supervisor policy as described in the operational guide; do not assume forced batcher shutdown interrupts SQLite I/O.

docs.title: Two bounded starting configurations
docs.text: These examples use the repository recipes for Async Batcher 0.3.0. Set up the matching recipe checkout; the examples modules are not part of the installed package. Choose the shape that matches who controls the producers. The numbers are demonstration limits; check the backend's count, payload, and concurrency limits before changing them.

docs.title: File importer: wait for capacity
docs.text:
The producer owns the input stream and can slow down. This complete example writes generated records to SQLite without creating a task or retaining a result for every input:

import asyncio
from pathlib import Path

from examples.recipes.sqlite_stream import write_stream
from examples.recipes.support import Document


async def records():
    for index in range(1000):
        yield Document(str(index), f"Record {index}")


async def main():
    report = await write_stream(records(), Path("import.sqlite"), batch_size=32, max_pending=64)
    print(report["completed_items"])


asyncio.run(main())

Save it as import_demo.py in the recipe checkout and run uv run --no-sync python import_demo.py. The recipe sets a queue limit of 64, one active writer batch, a 10 ms collection delay, and a 64 KiB encoded payload budget. map waits for admission and bounds consumed-but-not-yielded input to 64 items. SQLite commits each batch independently; cancellation or failure can leave earlier writes committed. Stable IDs update existing rows on replay. Use the resumable recipe for atomic byte checkpoints against immutable input. For a JSONL source, replace records() with read_jsonl(Path("documents.jsonl")) from examples.recipes.support.

docs.title: Interactive service: reject overload explicitly
docs.text:
The service cannot control when clients arrive. Use a finite waiting queue and return an overload response rather than accumulating unlimited waiting handlers. This complete ASGI application uses the existing lifespan-managed recipe and its deterministic demonstration predictor:

from pathlib import Path

from examples.recipes.fastapi_app import create_app

app = create_app(
    Path("service.sqlite"),
    batch_size=16,
    queue_size=64,
    max_queue_time=0.01,
    response_timeout=2,
    shutdown_grace=5,
    shutdown_force=1,
)

Save it as service_demo.py in the recipe checkout. The optional example-test group provides FastAPI and Uvicorn for this demo; it is not needed by the core library:

uv sync --locked --group example-test --python 3.12
uv run --no-sync uvicorn service_demo:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --workers 1

POST /predict accepts {"features":[1,2,3]} and returns {"score":2.3}. A full queue returns HTTP 503 with Retry-After; response expiry returns HTTP 504 while accepted work can still finish. One batch runs at a time per batcher. The two-second response budget includes waiting and processing; the 10 ms collection delay is not an end-to-end deadline. The shutdown budgets control waiting and escalation, not a guarantee that cancellation can stop external writes or running threads. Read the FastAPI guide before replacing the demo predictor with a model/client.

docs.title: What each bound covers
docs.text:
Limit Covers Does not cover max_batch_size Items in one dispatched batch Bytes per item or backend rate max_queue_size Items buffered for dispatch Active batches or external producer tasks map(max_pending=...) Consumed inputs whose results have not been yielded by that map Other maps/producers or source buffers concurrency Active batch processors on one batcher Other processes, groups, or SDK retry attempts

max_queue_size=-1 or 0 means unlimited. The core keeps these compatibility defaults; the examples choose finite values explicitly. Item limits do not establish a total memory bound. Validate input sizes and set server connection/body limits as appropriate. Multiple server workers have separate queues and batchers; their total backend demand adds up.

Start with one of these paths and measure actual batch sizes and outcomes. Add cost budgets for variable payload sizes, groups for incompatible requests, or coalescing for equivalent concurrent reads only when the workload needs them. Keep per-item tenant/model metadata explicit. For services that handle sensitive backend errors, consider log_exceptions=False; for a neutral batch context, see processor_context in the API guide. Neither option replaces request authorization or application logging policy.

docs.title: Public type contracts
docs.text: Async Batcher 0.3.0 includes a PEP 561 marker in its wheel and source distribution. Type checkers can read the library's inline annotations after a normal package installation. Use the version selector to match these contracts to your installed release.

docs.title: Inference and explicit types
docs.text:
AsyncBatcher[T, S] accepts inputs of type T and returns S from process(). Its bounded map() iterator yields the same result type. from_callable() infers these parameters from an annotated synchronous or asynchronous processor:

from typing import assert_type

from async_batcher import AsyncBatcher


async def render(items: list[int]) -> list[str]:
    return [str(item) for item in items]


batcher = AsyncBatcher.from_callable(
    render,
    max_batch_size=32,
    max_batch_cost=100,
    item_cost=lambda item: 1,
)
assert_type(batcher, AsyncBatcher[int, str])


async def use_batcher() -> None:
    async with batcher:
        assert_type(await batcher.process(1), str)
        async for result in batcher.map([1, 2, 3], max_pending=8):
            assert_type(result, str)

A processor returning only None produces AsyncBatcher[T, None]. A processor that may return either results or None produces an optional result type. Per-item Exception and asyncio.CancelledError values are raised for their callers, so they are not successful result types. Annotate a processor's return type to express those alternatives accurately.

Processors can return ordered, sized iterables, including custom containers with __len__ and __iter__. Runtime checks still reject unordered containers, mappings, text, and a result count that differs from the batch size. Type checking does not replace those checks or the runtime validation of positive limits and finite costs. Ordinary integer and float costs, as well as numbers.Real implementations such as Fraction, are accepted.

The result parameter is covariant: a batcher returning str can be used where one returning object is required. Inputs remain invariant. GroupedBatcher[K, T, S] carries the group-key, input, and result types separately. BatcherStats and BatchEvent are immutable typed snapshots; monitoring callbacks must be synchronous and return None.

docs.title: Checking changes
docs.text:
The dedicated typecheck group pins mypy independently of optional SDK stubs in the typing group. Run the same installed-package check as CI:

uv sync --locked --no-default-groups --group typecheck
uv run --no-sync python .github/scripts/check_public_typing.py

The helper builds and installs a wheel in an isolated temporary environment, then checks strict consumer examples outside the checkout. Positive examples assert inferred types. Negative examples require exact error locations and codes for invalid inputs, incompatible callbacks, unknown options, and mutation of immutable snapshots. Removing the installed py.typed marker must also make the positive example fail. Distribution checks independently verify the marker in the direct wheel and the wheel rebuilt from the source distribution.

The core gate covers public callable, streaming, grouping, and observability APIs. Kafka and Kinesis have additional installed-wheel consumer checks, run in their adapter CI jobs:

uv run --no-sync python .github/scripts/check_public_typing.py --adapter kafka
uv run --no-sync python .github/scripts/check_public_typing.py --adapter aws

After syncing the typecheck group above, these commands export the selected extra from uv.lock and install its exact, hash-checked dependencies into a separate temporary environment. The AWS check also installs the existing locked typing stub group. The main environment and core-only CI jobs remain free of optional SDKs.

These checks verify record inputs, core keyword options, callback types, mapped results, and SDK metadata. Kafka results are RecordMetadata | None, preserving the producer's acks=0 behavior. The gate reads aiokafka's inline annotations using mypy's narrowly scoped follow_untyped_imports option because the locked SDK does not ship a py.typed marker; metadata field assertions prevent an unnoticed fallback to Any. Kinesis acknowledgements keep the existing dict[str, Any] contract for service response fields. Unknown keywords and incompatible input or result types must produce exact diagnostics; no missing-import errors are suppressed.

This does not claim strict checking of every private implementation or other optional SDK adapter. The checker remains a development dependency; installing the core library adds no runtime dependencies.

docs.title: Variable-length token inference
docs.text:
This runnable recipe groups compatible token rows, pads each batch, calls a synchronous model once, and restores each request's original output length. It needs only the core package and standard library. The included model doubles token IDs for a demonstration; it is not trained and does not produce semantic predictions. The example lives in the repository, outside the installed package. From the matching recipe checkout:

uv sync --locked --no-default-groups --python 3.12
uv run --no-sync python -m examples.recipes.variable_inference

The finite 32-request cohort prints actual model-call shapes, completed requests, and elapsed time through group drain. These are observations of the demo, not an inference speedup claim. The histogram retains counts for bounded (rows, padded_width) combinations, not token payloads.

docs.title: Preserve inputs and restore outputs
docs.text:
TokenRequest snapshots a list/tuple of nonnegative integer token IDs into an immutable tuple. It also carries immutable request ID, tenant, and model revision. Empty sequences are rejected; choose an explicit application policy for them before submission. No tokenizer is downloaded or implied: use the vocabulary and special-token policy for your actual model.

collate preserves row order and pads to the longest row in that batch, using zero padding. Its attention mask uses original lengths, so a real zero token is still marked as input. Change the padding convention before using a model that requires a different pad token.

For example, token rows (0, 2) and (7,) become:

Field First row Second row input_ids (0, 2) (7, 0) attention_mask (1, 1) (1, 0) Demo model output (0, 4) (14, 0) Routed TokenPrediction.values (0, 4) (14,)

The synchronous model receives one immutable ModelBatch. It must return a list/tuple with one list/tuple of finite numeric values for every padded row. This example is token-level scalar prediction; adapt another output head explicitly. Convert arrays/tensors with the appropriate .tolist() operation before returning, and validate the expected dimensions in that adapter.

The recipe validates the complete padded output, including discarded padding positions, before returning any result. Wrong row counts, wrong widths, nonnumeric or nonfinite values fail the whole batch. unbatch then trims to original lengths and attaches each original request ID. A borrowed async result is not awaited or cancelled; use a separate async-model recipe instead of returning awaitables from this synchronous callback.

docs.title: Budget for padding, not just input token totals
docs.text:
Summing raw lengths can underestimate padded work: lengths 1 and 16 contain 17 tokens, but a dense two-row batch occupies 32 token positions. The recipe uses increasing length buckets (16, 64, 256) and charges the bucket ceiling for every item, using the core item_cost callback.

For a group with ceiling B and N requests, the actual padded width is at most B. The cost check enforces N × B <= padded_token_budget, so actual padded positions also fit that budget. With the default 256-position budget and count limit 16:

Bucket ceiling Maximum rows from the cost budget Maximum rows after the count limit 16 16 16 64 4 4 256 1 1

All configured buckets must fit the budget. An item above the largest bucket fails before creating a group or calling the model. Split oversized documents upstream only if you can define how their chunk predictions should be recombined; the recipe does not silently truncate or change one request into several independent results.

The estimate is deliberately conservative: a short row near the bottom of a bucket consumes its full ceiling. Choose finer buckets to reduce waste, while accounting for more partially filled groups and the max_groups limit. The 10 ms collection delay still dispatches partial batches. Count, cost, queue age, and per-group concurrency limits apply together.

Padded token positions are not a GPU-memory limit. Input tensors, attention masks, output heads, dtype, hidden activations, caches, and model weights also use memory. Attention work may scale nonlinearly with sequence length. Profile the actual model and device before choosing ceilings, budgets, and concurrency; leave room for fixed overhead and other workloads.

docs.title: Keep incompatible work and resources separate
docs.text:
The group key contains tenant, model revision, and length bucket. Add other compatibility settings when they affect a shared call, such as vocabulary, normalization, output-head selection, or a backend destination. Authenticate requests before submission; group keys are not authorization. Bind immutable model/client configuration instead of changing shared state between tenants. Children use an explicit empty processor context and metadata-only failure logging, so the first request's ambient context and exception text do not become shared model context or log payloads. Pass required service information explicitly in model configuration or ModelBatch.

All child batchers borrow the same caller-owned ThreadPoolExecutor, so max_workers bounds simultaneously executing synchronous calls across groups. The demo uses one worker. Keep the model alive until that executor has joined; forced batcher shutdown cannot interrupt a running inference thread. The helper neither closes the model nor shuts down the pool.

import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

from examples.recipes.variable_inference import DemoTokenModel, TokenRequest, inference_groups


async def main(pool):
    model = DemoTokenModel()  # Replace with a synchronous ModelBatch -> dense rows callable.
    async with inference_groups(model, executor=pool, padded_token_budget=256) as groups:
        cohort = [
            TokenRequest("first", "tenant-a", "demo-v1", [1, 2, 3]),
            TokenRequest("second", "tenant-a", "demo-v1", [4]),
        ]
        print(await asyncio.gather(*(groups.process(item) for item in cohort)))


with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as pool:
    asyncio.run(main(pool))

This uses a small finite cohort. Do not create one task per item for an unbounded source. Bound producers and admission, and remember that each child here has a 64-item waiting queue. Group slots, queues, and a shared executor limit different resources; the executor's submission queue is not a complete backpressure policy. See group ownership, cost budgets, and the workload guide.

docs.title: Choose batching for your workload
docs.text: Start with package installation. The core has no runtime dependencies; install an adapter extra only when you use that backend.

docs.title: Check the backend contract first
docs.text:
Batching helps when a bulk call amortizes network, transaction, or model overhead. A function that simply performs the same independent calls in sequence may add latency without reducing that work. Measure your own end-to-end latency and throughput; the included benchmarks do not predict a particular database or model's performance.

Before choosing limits, identify:

  • The backend's maximum record count and encoded byte/token limits, including fixed request overhead.
  • Which items can share one call: destination, operation, model revision, schema, and authentication.
  • Whether results preserve input order, and how missing, duplicate, or failed results are identified.
  • Which effects can already have happened when a request fails or its caller is cancelled.
  • Who owns the client, model, executor, and any durable replay/checkpoint state.

Use a built-in adapter when its operation and failure contract fit. Otherwise, wrap a bulk function with from_callable, return one result per item, and use map for bounded producers. A batcher does not make a backend transactional, enforce a request-rate limit, or persist queued work across a process crash.

docs.title: Choose a starting shape
docs.text:
Start with the two bounded configurations for a runnable importer or interactive service before adding composition options.

Workload First configuration decisions Interactive HTTP/RPC Choose a short collection delay from the latency budget, a finite waiting queue, and an explicit overload response. Account for backend time separately. See FastAPI and operational deadlines. File or message stream For broker deliveries, see acknowledgement and replay. Bound map(max_pending=...), keep the source lazy, and consume results as they arrive. Choose ordered results only if needed. See the cookbook and resumable file importer. Database writes Respect the adapter's transaction boundaries. Use stable record IDs and define replay behavior; concurrency can reorder commits. Model inference Collate variable-length inputs, group compatible model/input shapes, and reserve memory for padding and outputs. A token count is an estimate, not a GPU memory measurement. Embedding pipeline Bound both stages and keep IDs attached to vectors. Validate model dimensions and the destination namespace before writing. See the Cohere-to-Pinecone recipe.

Keep max_pending large enough for the intended batch if latency allows. Smaller windows still work, but normally dispatch partial batches at the collection deadline. Queue and pending limits count items; they do not bound each item's size or all upstream HTTP handlers.

Set a backend-safe count limit first. Add a conservative cost budget when item sizes vary, then choose finite queue/pending limits and backend concurrency. Observe actual batch sizes and outcomes before tuning. max_queue_time measures collection delay from the oldest item; time waiting for an active batch, backend I/O, and response serialization can make total latency longer.

docs.title: Preserve immutable routing metadata
docs.text:
Put per-request information in each submitted item. For example:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PredictionRequest:
    tenant_id: str
    model_revision: str
    text: str


def compatibility_key(request: PredictionRequest) -> tuple[str, str]:
    return request.tenant_id, request.model_revision

The strings above are immutable. frozen=True alone does not freeze a nested list, dictionary, or client object: copy or normalize mutable input before submitting it, or retain exclusive ownership until processing finishes. Cost estimates are cached once per submission; changing the payload afterward can invalidate the budget and change what the backend receives.

Derive a GroupedBatcher key from every setting that must be shared within one backend call. Depending on the API, that can include tenant, namespace, model revision, normalization policy, vector dimension, operation, or schema version. Bind that configuration into the child factory instead of changing a shared client's destination between requests. Bound the number of groups; each child has its own queue and concurrency limit.

Validate authorization before submission. A tenant key separates work; it does not authenticate the caller. Avoid putting credentials or mutable request objects in group keys, exceptions, or monitoring labels. Keep high-cardinality IDs out of metric labels.

A processor runs once for a batch. Ambient ContextVar values are not a per-item metadata channel: requests with different tenant or tracing values can otherwise observe one batch's context. Carry essential metadata explicitly, even when using a separate processor context policy.

docs.title: Own configuration and cleanup
docs.text:
Treat constructor options and a child factory's backend configuration as construction-only settings. Direct attribute assignment is not a supported reconfiguration API; queues and semaphores have already been created. To change settings, close application intake, drain the old batcher, create its replacement, and then reopen intake. Coordinate that switch with producers instead of mutating a live shared instance.

Keep client/model/executor contexts outside the batcher context so they outlive its work. A normal context exit drains without an implicit timeout. Forced cancellation cannot interrupt an already running Python thread or prove that an external write did not happen; preserve those resources until their actual work has ended. See lifecycle and executors. The operational recipes demonstrate bounded drain/escalation, one backend capacity limit across groups, and a telemetry exporter with explicit overflow accounting.

For an unsupported workload, open a use-case issue with a small payload example, backend limits, failure semantics, and measured requirements. Remove secrets and private customer data before sharing examples.
